question.text: In the opposite figure: ABCD is a quadrilateral, its diagonals intersect at E, m(∠ACB) = 58°, m(∠CAD) = 35°, m(∠CED) = 93°. Can a circle be drawn passing through the vertices of the quadrilateral ABCD? Explain your answer?

answers.answer: Yes, a circle can be drawn, because m(∠ADB) = m(∠ACB) = 58° on the base AB in one direction of it.
solution: Angle CED is an exterior angle of triangle AED, so m(∠CED) = m(∠CAD) + m(∠ADE).
Also m(∠ACB) = 58°.
So m(∠ADB) = m(∠ACB) = 58°.
They are two drawn angles on the base AB, and C and D are on the same side of AB (one direction).
Therefore ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, so a circle can pass through A, B, C and D.

checks.resolve_answer: Yes. In triangle AED, m(∠AED) = 180° - 93° = 87°, so m(∠ADB) = 180° - 35° - 87° = 58°. Then m(∠ADB) = m(∠ACB) = 58°, and they are two drawn angles on the base AB and in one direction of it. So ABCD is cyclic and a circle can pass through its vertices.

question.text: Which of the following figures is a cyclic quadrilateral? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: Yes, Figure 1 is a cyclic quadrilateral because m(∠DAC) = m(∠DBC) = 50°.
solution: The diagonals are perpendicular at E, so in triangle ADE: m(∠DAC) = 90° − 40° = 50°.
m(∠DBC) = 50° (given in the figure).
So m(∠DAC) = m(∠DBC) = 50°.
They are two drawn angles on the base DC and in one direction of it.
Therefore Figure 1 is a cyclic quadrilateral.

question.text: Which of the following figures is a cyclic quadrilateral? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: No, Figure 3 is not a cyclic quadrilateral because m(∠DAC) = 40° but m(∠DBC) = 41°.
solution: DA ∥ CB, so m(∠DBC) = m(∠ADB) = 41° (alternate angles).
In triangle ADE: m(∠DAC) = 180° − 41° − 99° = 40°.
On the base DC, m(∠DAC) = 40° and m(∠DBC) = 41° are not equal.
So Figure 3 is not a cyclic quadrilateral.

question.text: Which of the following figures is a cyclic quadrilateral? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: No, Figure 4 is not a cyclic quadrilateral.
solution: Figure 4 is a parallelogram whose angles are not right angles.
In it, m(∠DAC) = m(∠ACB) (alternate angles).

That would make the diagonals equal, which holds only for a rectangle.
Figure 4 is not a rectangle, so it is not cyclic.

question.text: Which of the following figures is a cyclic quadrilateral? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: Yes, Figure 5 is a cyclic quadrilateral.
solution: DA ∥ CB and DC = AB, so Figure 5 is an isosceles trapezium and m(∠DCB) = m(∠ABC).
In triangles DCB and ABC: DC = AB, CB is common and m(∠DCB) = m(∠ABC).
So the triangles are congruent, and m(∠CDB) = m(∠CAB).
They are two drawn angles on the base CB and in one direction of it.
Therefore Figure 5 is a cyclic quadrilateral.

question.text: In the previous example, where is the center of the circle passing through the vertices of the figure AXBY? located? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: The centre is the midpoint of AY, because AY is a diameter of the circle through A, X, B and Y.
solution: From the example, m(∠AXY) = 90° and m(∠ABY) = 90°.
An inscribed angle of 90° stands on a diameter.
So the base AY is a diameter of the circle passing through A, X, B and Y.
The centre of a circle lies at the midpoint of its diameter.
So the centre is the midpoint of AY.

checks.resolve_answer: The centre is the midpoint of AY. The angles AXY and ABY are both right angles, so AY is a diameter of the circle through A, X, B and Y. The centre is therefore the midpoint of AY.

question.text: In the opposite figure: A circle with center M. X and Y are the two midpoints of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ respectively. Prove that:

answers.answer: AXYM is a cyclic quadrilateral because m(∠AXM) = m(∠AYM) = 90°.
solution: X is the midpoint of AB and M is the centre, so MX ⊥ AB and m(∠AXM) = 90°.
Y is the midpoint of AC, so MY ⊥ AC and m(∠AYM) = 90°.
So m(∠AXM) = m(∠AYM) = 90°.
They are two drawn angles on the base AM and in one direction of it.
Therefore AXYM is a cyclic quadrilateral.

checks.resolve_answer: X is the midpoint of AB, so MX ⊥ AB and m(∠AXM) = 90°. Y is the midpoint of AC, so MY ⊥ AC and m(∠AYM) = 90°. These are two equal angles on the base AM and in one direction of it, so AXYM is a cyclic quadrilateral.

question.text: In the opposite figure: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral which has $\overrightarrow{AE}$ bisects $\angle BAC$ and $\overrightarrow{DF}$ bisects $\angle BDC$. Prove that:

answers.answer: AEFD is a cyclic quadrilateral because m(∠EAF) = m(∠EDF).
solution: m(∠BAC) = m(∠BDC), since both are inscribed on the arc BC.
AE bisects ∠BAC, so m(∠EAF) = ½ m(∠BAC).
DF bisects ∠BDC, so m(∠EDF) = ½ m(∠BDC).
So m(∠EAF) = m(∠EDF).
They are two drawn angles on the base EF and in one direction of it.
Therefore AEFD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

checks.resolve_answer: m(∠BAC) = m(∠BDC) because both are inscribed angles on arc BC. Their halves are equal, so m(∠EAF) = m(∠EDF). These are two angles on the base EF and in one direction of it, so AEFD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

question.text: In the opposite figure: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral which has $\overrightarrow{AE}$ bisects $\angle BAC$ and $\overrightarrow{DF}$ bisects $\angle BDC$. Prove that:

answers.answer: EF ∥ BC, because the corresponding angles AFE and ACB are equal.
solution: AEFD is cyclic (First), so m(∠AFE) = m(∠ADE), as both are inscribed on the arc AE.
m(∠ADB) = m(∠ACB), since both are inscribed on the arc AB of circle ABCD.
So m(∠AFE) = m(∠ACB).
These are corresponding angles for lines EF and BC with transversal AC.
Therefore EF ∥ BC.

checks.resolve_answer: AEFD is cyclic, so m(∠AFE) = m(∠ADE) = m(∠ADB) (both on the base AE). Also m(∠ADB) = m(∠ACB) (both inscribed on arc AB). So m(∠AFE) = m(∠ACB). These are corresponding angles for EF and BC with transversal AC, so EF ∥ BC.
